lesson.title: Saturated, Unsaturated, and Supersaturated: Reading How Full a Solution Is
lesson.summary: A solution is unsaturated, saturated, or supersaturated depending on how its dissolved solute compares to the solubility limit at that temperature, with saturation itself being a dynamic equilibrium between dissolving and recrystallizing.
lesson.body:
Once a solute's solubility limit at a given temperature is known, any actual solution can be sorted into one of three states relative to that limit. An unsaturated solution holds less solute than the maximum and can still dissolve more. A saturated solution holds exactly the maximum, in dynamic equilibrium with any undissolved excess solute sitting at the bottom. A supersaturated solution, unusually, holds more solute than the equilibrium maximum allows, an unstable condition that exists only because nothing has triggered it to release the excess yet.

At saturation, nothing looks like it is happening, but at the molecular level plenty is: solute particles are continuously leaving the undissolved solid and entering solution while, at the exact same rate, dissolved particles are recrystallizing back onto the solid. That balance is the same kind of dynamic equilibrium introduced for vapor pressure, just applied to dissolving instead of evaporating.

Using sodium chloride's solubility of about 36 g per 100 g of water at 20°C from the last chapter, the three states become easy to tell apart with real numbers. Dissolve 20 g of NaCl in 100 g of water at 20°C: since 20 g is less than the 36 g maximum, the solution is unsaturated, and it could still accept 36 g minus 20 g, or 16 more grams, before reaching its limit. Now try adding 45 g of NaCl to a fresh 100 g of water at the same temperature: only 36 g will actually dissolve, no matter how long you stir, leaving 45 g minus 36 g, or 9 g, sitting undissolved at the bottom. That solution is saturated, confirmed visibly by the leftover solid in equilibrium with the dissolved portion.

Supersaturation takes a different path to get there. Dissolve solute at a higher temperature, where solubility is greater, then cool the solution slowly and without disturbing it. If no solid crystal forms to give the excess solute somewhere to land, more solute can remain dissolved than the cooler temperature's solubility would normally allow, a metastable state that persists only until something interrupts it: a stray dust particle, a scratch on the container, or a single seed crystal dropped in. Any of those can trigger the excess solute to crystallize out rapidly, which is the basis of both rock candy and the reusable heat packs that click and release warmth as a supersaturated sodium acetate solution suddenly recrystallizes.
